investment_summary:
Netflix grew 2025 revenue 16% to $45.18 billion and lifted operating margin to 29.5% from 26.7% [1]. Net income rose 26% to $10.98 billion, and free cash flow reached $9.46 billion [1]. Momentum is broad: APAC grew 21% and EMEA 17% in reported terms [1].

Valuation is the constraint. The reverse DCF implies 17.2% annual revenue growth for ten years, above 13.1% FY2026 consensus and a 12.6% three-year historical CAGR [2][3]. At that price, the implied return is 8.2% against a 12.9% WACC [2][3]. Consensus is a Buy with an $84.55 mean target [3].

The main risk is the WBD deal: $42.2 billion of bridge commitments against $14.5 billion of existing notes could cut buybacks and reverse deleveraging [1]. Net cash moved to -$6.91 billion by 30 September 2026 [2]. Consensus and balance-sheet figures are dated after the 10-K. Growth must stay near consensus, and cash flow must keep funding repurchases.
key_takeaways: Margin expansion should continue as content costs scale slower than revenue: operating margin rose to 29.5% from 26.7% [1].
The WBD deal is the main swing factor: $42.2 billion of bridge commitments could reverse the deleveraging and slow buybacks [1].
Shares look fully valued: the current enterprise value implies 17.2% revenue growth for ten years versus 13.1% FY2026 consensus [2][3].
Buybacks are shrinking the share count, but free cash flow of $9.46 billion must keep covering repurchases plus debt repayments [1][2].
business_overview:
Netflix, Inc. is one of the world's leading entertainment services, offering TV series, films, games and live programming across genres and languages on monthly membership plans [1]. Paid plans range from $1 to $37 per month by country, and an ad-supported plan widens the entry price point [1]. The company reports as one operating segment and competes for consumers' leisure time with linear TV, piracy, video games, user-generated content and social media [1]. Revenue reached $45.18 billion in 2025, up 16% from $39.00 billion (17% in constant currency) [1]. Operating income rose 28% to $13.33 billion, lifting operating margin to 29.5% from 26.7% in 2024 and 20.6% in 2023 [1]. Net income grew 26% to $10.98 billion, and diluted EPS rose 28% to $2.53 [1]. Netflix also runs its own Open Connect content delivery network, which gives it control over streaming delivery costs [1]. The company stopped reporting paid membership counts in 2025, so the filing does not allow member growth to be measured [1].

The model is cash-generative and returns capital to shareholders. Operating cash flow rose to $10.15 billion from $7.36 billion, and free cash flow reached $9.46 billion after $688 million of capital expenditure [1][2]. Netflix repurchased 86.5 million shares for $9.1 billion in 2025 and has $8.0 billion of authorization remaining [1]. Diluted share count fell 1.1% over the year, and total debt was reduced to $14.46 billion from $15.58 billion after $1.83 billion of repayments [1]. Liquidity is adequate, with $9.06 billion of cash and short-term investments and an undrawn $3 billion revolver [1][2]. Content is the largest cost: content amortization rose $1.12 billion, and content obligations total $24.04 billion, most of them multi-year and fixed [1].

The defining strategic event is the agreed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. Signed on December 4, 2025 and amended on January 19, 2026, the deal pays $27.75 in cash per share, for an equity value of about $72.0 billion and an enterprise value of about $82.7 billion, with closing expected 12 to 18 months after signing [1]. The bridge facility has been raised to $42.2 billion [1]. As of 26 November 2026, consensus rates the stock Buy with a mean target of $84.55 (range $57 to $126), a view dated after the 10-K [3].
market_position:
Netflix's streaming revenue is spread across four regions, and the United States and Canada remain the largest. UCAN revenue rose 15% to $19.96 billion, or 44.2% of the total, from $17.36 billion [1]. EMEA revenue rose 17% to $14.51 billion (32.1% of the total), with constant-currency growth of 16% [1]. Latin America grew 11% to $5.36 billion (11.9% of the total), but 23% in constant currency, because currency translation cut about 12 points from reported growth [1]. Asia-Pacific was the fastest-growing region, up 21% to $5.35 billion (11.8% of the total) [1]. Shares are calculated from reported regional revenue, since the filing does not disclose market share [1].

The growth profile is shifting outward. EMEA and APAC grew 17% and 21% on a reported basis, and LATAM grew 23% in constant currency, so the fastest momentum sits outside North America [1]. Netflix's position rests on original and exclusive programming, and the filing cites partner billing through cable and telecom set-top boxes as a distribution advantage [1]. Netflix names no major customers because revenue comes from individual members [1]. Advertising is an emerging stream: the company describes its ad business as having limited operating history [1]. Regulation is adding costs, with countries introducing investment obligations, levies and content quotas [1].

Position is strongest where the content library is deep, but the cost of holding it is rising. Brazilian non-income tax assessments added $1.12 billion to other cost of revenues in 2025, a charge management says will not materially affect future results [1]. Consensus FY2026 revenue of $51.13 billion (up 13.1%) implies the regional growth momentum is expected to continue [3]. The consensus valuation uses a price of $59.41, about 29% below the $83.54 close on the filing date [2][3].
operating_results:
Netflix's 2025 revenue rose 16% to $45.18 billion from $39.00 billion, and constant-currency growth was 17%, so currency was a modest drag on the reported figure [1]. Cost of revenues grew 11% to $23.28 billion and fell to 52% of revenue from 54%, so gross profit expanded faster than sales. The result was an operating margin of 29.5%, up from 26.7% in 2024 and 20.6% in 2023, with operating income up 28% to $13.33 billion [1]. Net income rose 26% to $10.98 billion, a 24.3% net margin against 22.3% a year earlier, and diluted EPS reached $2.53, up 28% from $1.98 [1]. Part of the EPS gain came from buybacks: the diluted share count fell 1.1% after $9.1 billion of repurchases [1].

The margin gain was not free of pressure. Other cost of revenues rose $1.12 billion, driven mainly by Brazilian non-income tax assessments, which management says will not materially affect future results [1]. Content amortization rose $1.12 billion over the year, and total content obligations reached $24.04 billion, most of which are multi-year and largely fixed [1]. The tax provision rose 39% to $1.74 billion, lifting the effective rate to 14%, and interest expense rose 8% [1]. Because these costs sit in the cost base, the 2025 margin holds only if content spending keeps growing more slowly than revenue.

Cash generation supports the earnings figures. Operating cash flow rose to $10.15 billion from $7.36 billion, and free cash flow reached $9.46 billion after $688 million of capital expenditure [1][2]. Free cash flow conversion on the peer-analysis basis rose to 0.86 in 2025 from 0.79, although the filing data does not define that measure [4]. Looking forward, consensus expects FY2026 revenue of $51.13 billion (up 13.1%) and EPS of $3.57, with the current-year EPS estimate down 0.3% over 90 days [3]. These consensus figures are dated after the 10-K, so they are expectations rather than reported results.
risk_assessment:
Netflix's risk profile centers on three linked exposures. The first is member retention in a fiercely competitive market. The filing describes entertainment video as "intensely competitive and subject to rapid change," with rivals ranging from broadcasters and cable operators to piracy services [1]. Cancellations are tied to households cutting expenses or feeling they do not use the service enough, and the advertising business, which has limited operating history, is still unproven [1]. The filing does not quantify churn, so the size of this risk cannot be measured from the 10-K alone.

The second risk is leverage combined with fixed content commitments and the WBD transaction. Senior notes total about $14.5 billion, the $3 billion revolver is undrawn, and the WBD commitments include a $42.2 billion senior unsecured bridge term loan, a $5 billion revolver and a $20 billion delayed draw term loan [1]. The filing warns that the company may be unable to cut streaming content obligations quickly if cash flow falls, and that refinancing could come at higher rates with more onerous covenants [1]. If the deal does not complete, a $5.8 billion termination fee could be payable, equal to about 40% of existing notes [1]. Post-closing regulatory conditions could also force significant operational adjustments [1]. Liquidity is adequate today, with $9.06 billion of cash and short-term investments at year-end [2], but net cash had moved to -$6.91 billion by 30 September 2026 [2].

The third risk is labor disruption. The WGA agreement expires May 1, 2026, and the SAG-AFTRA and DGA agreements expire June 30, 2026 [1]. The filing notes that work stoppages have halted productions before, so this exposure is dated and has occurred in the past. The company may not be indemnified or insured against certain content liabilities, and the filing does not describe a contractual protection against production stoppages [1]. Two further items are cybersecurity and cloud concentration. The company does not carry insurance for cybersecurity disruption and says it "cannot easily switch" its AWS operations to another provider [1].

Several developments would reduce these risks: guild renewals before expiry, a WBD closing on covenant-light terms, and continued revenue growth in mature markets. A revenue decline together with a revolver draw would confirm the linkage between the three risks [1]. Consensus rates the stock Buy, but its target range of $57 to $126 shows wide disagreement about the outcome, and that view is dated after the 10-K [3].
competitors_analysis:
Netflix compares favorably with its three peers on margins and returns. Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD), Paramount Skydance (PSKY) and Disney (DIS) were chosen because they combine studio production with direct-to-consumer streaming, the closest business-model match in the candidate list. Disney is about twice Netflix's size and serves as the scale benchmark [4]. In 2025 Netflix's gross margin was 48.5%, against 44.0% for WBD and 37.8% for Disney, while Paramount's margin was 29.6% in 2024, the latest year reported [4]. Netflix's EBITDA margin was 67.0%, against 57.0% for WBD and 20.3% for Disney [4]. Return on invested capital was 28.4% for Netflix, against 4.0% for WBD and 6.8% for Disney in 2025, and Netflix's ROIC has risen every year since 2022 [4].

Revenue growth is the clearest gap. Netflix grew revenue 15.9% in 2025 to $45.18 billion, while WBD revenue fell 5.1% to $37.30 billion, and Paramount's revenue declined in 2023 and 2024 [4]. Netflix is the only one of the four to grow more than 15% in both 2024 and 2025 [4]. Disney's free cash flow of $10.08 billion in 2025 exceeded Netflix's $9.46 billion, so Netflix is not the largest cash generator in absolute terms [4]. Its FCF conversion of 0.86 in 2025 was slightly above Disney's 0.81, although the conversion definition is not stated in the data [4].

Valuation is where the comparison is less favorable. Netflix trades at 13.3 times 2025 EBITDA, close to Disney's 12.8 times, but its EV/Sales of 8.9 compares with Disney's 2.6 because its margin is about three times higher [4]. The EV/EBITDA multiple has nearly doubled from 6.9 times in 2022, so the market already prices in much of the margin gain [4]. Peer valuation data for WBD and Paramount is not available, so the comparison cannot be extended to them [4]. Consensus, dated after the 10-K, shows a FY2026 forward EV/Sales of 5.0 times for Netflix, below the trailing figure [3].

The comparison has limits. The filing data does not define FCF conversion, gross margin or EBITDA on a consistent basis, so the peer figures are indicative [4]. WBD is also the target of Netflix's pending acquisition, so its standalone figures will change if the deal completes [1].

investment_theses.thesis: Operating margin stays above 29% in 2026 as content amortization grows slower than revenue.
investment_theses.evidence: Operating margin rose to 29.5% from 26.7%, and cost of revenues fell to 52% of revenue from 54% [1]. FY2026 consensus revenue is $51.13 billion, up 13.1% [3].
investment_theses.signpost: Q4 2026 results (January 2027): full-year 2026 operating margin at or above 29%.
investment_theses.invalidation: Full-year 2026 operating margin falls back below 2025's 29.5%, or cost of revenues rises above 2025's 52% of revenue.

investment_theses.thesis: The WBD financing will absorb cash that would otherwise fund buybacks, so the 2027 repurchase pace falls below 2025's $9.1 billion.
investment_theses.evidence: Senior notes total about $14.5 billion and the $3 billion revolver is undrawn, against a $42.2 billion bridge, a $20 billion delayed draw term loan and a $5 billion revolver [1]. Net cash moved to -$6.91 billion at 30 September 2026 [2].
investment_theses.signpost: Q1 2027 results (April 2027) and the WBD closing update: repurchases below $9.1 billion annualized and debt drawn under the bridge.
investment_theses.invalidation: The deal closes on unsecured, covenant-light terms, and repurchases continue at or above $9 billion a year while net debt falls.

investment_theses.thesis: The current price needs growth above consensus for a decade, so returns are below the cost of capital unless growth beats expectations.
investment_theses.evidence: The reverse DCF implies 17.2% annual revenue growth for ten years, versus 13.1% and 10.7% consensus for FY2026 and FY2027 and a 12.6% three-year historical CAGR [2][3]. The implied IRR is 8.2% against a 12.9% WACC [2][3].
investment_theses.signpost: Q4 2026 results (January 2027): FY2026 revenue at or above $51.1 billion, and FY2027 EPS consensus of $3.76 held or raised.
investment_theses.invalidation: Revenue growth holds at or above 17% in FY2026 and FY2027 consensus EPS is raised, which would make the implied growth achievable.

investment_theses.thesis: Free cash flow will keep covering buybacks, but only if operating cash flow grows faster than content spending.
investment_theses.evidence: FY2025 free cash flow was $9.46 billion, against $9.13 billion of buybacks and $1.83 billion of debt repayments, so financing outflows of $10.35 billion exceeded free cash flow [1]. Trailing free cash flow was $11.38 billion at 30 September 2026 [2].
investment_theses.signpost: Trailing twelve-month free cash flow above $11 billion at each quarter-end through Q4 2026.
investment_theses.invalidation: Trailing free cash flow falls below annual buybacks of about $9 billion while repurchases continue at the same pace.
